note: Rewritten to the claim that survived the four independent audits.

problems.original_statement: One person's treatment can change another's outcome through infection, provider behavior, household exposure or a shared resource constraint. Target trial emulation as normally practiced assumes this does not happen. Methods under partial interference define direct and spillover effects and are well developed in their own literature, but they are rarely joined to emulation, and the join is not cosmetic: eligibility, assignment and positivity all become cluster- or network-dependent quantities. Cloning individuals independently, which is the standard device for grace periods, can assign a set of clones a joint strategy that no cluster could actually receive, so the artificial censoring is then censoring on an impossible world. The TARGET reporting guideline currently offers no cluster-trial extension.
problems.correction_note: The account of cloning was imprecise. Cloning creates strategy-specific copies of an individual; it does not itself assign a realized joint allocation to a cluster. The failure is in intervention definition, consistency and joint positivity when individual strategies are read as a joint allocation, not in the artificial censoring operating on an impossible world.
problems.statement: One person's treatment can change another's outcome through infection, provider behavior, household exposure or a shared resource constraint. Target trial emulation as normally practiced invokes no interference, and under that assumption an individual-level protocol is coherent. Identifying a direct or spillover effect requires more than adding the interference literature alongside it: the emulation has to specify a feasible joint or stochastic treatment policy, the exposure mapping or potential-outcome indexing that defines what each unit is exposed to, and joint support for that exposure. Individual clone-censor rules do not identify those effects, because a set of individually compatible strategies need not correspond to any allocation a cluster could receive. Eligibility, assignment and positivity all become cluster- or network-dependent quantities, and the TARGET reporting guideline offers no cluster-trial extension.
problems.why_open: There is no canonical exposure mapping: own treatment plus treated-neighbor proportion is one choice among many, and different choices give different and equally valid effects, so the estimand has to be argued rather than derived. Positivity must hold for the joint neighborhood exposure, which is far stronger than individual positivity and typically fails in observed networks. Networks are measured with error, and contagion, homophily and spillover are only weakly separable even when the network is known exactly.
problems.proposed_direction: Define network target trials in which the exposure mapping and the feasible joint or stochastic policy are protocol components rather than analysis conveniences, and state the positivity condition for the joint exposure explicitly. Develop cluster-level clone-censor-weighting, in which compatibility is judged for the allocation a cluster could receive rather than for each individual, alongside network targeted learning and agent-based g-computation. Test sensitivity to network mismeasurement by deleting edges at known rates, since a method correct on a perfect network and silent on a noisy one is not usable.

problems.original_statement: An internally valid estimate need not apply to the health system, population or calendar period where the decision will be made. Weighting, outcome modeling and doubly robust transport estimators all exist, and all of them require that the effect modifiers be measured, that the populations overlap, and that effects be conditionally exchangeable across samples. Applied transport work still mostly uses conventional sampling weights or outcome models despite the more flexible alternatives. The deeper issue is that transporting an observational estimate stacks the sampling-exchangeability assumption on top of the treatment-exchangeability assumption, and no current reporting practice shows how the two compound or which one a given discrepancy should be charged to.
problems.correction_note: Identification does not require that every effect modifier be measured; it requires a sufficient set. Modifiers that do not differ across populations, or that are irrelevant after conditioning, need not be observed. Transport estimators are also reaching emulation practice faster than the entry allowed, including inside benchmarking programs.
problems.statement: An internally valid estimate need not apply to the health system, population or calendar period where the decision will be made. Transporting an observational contrast requires treatment exchangeability in the source, effect exchangeability across samples conditional on a sufficient measured set, and positivity for both treatment and sampling. A sufficient set is weaker than every effect modifier: modifiers that do not differ across populations or that are irrelevant after conditioning need not be observed. Transport estimators are now being applied to emulations, including post hoc standardization of emulations to their trial populations inside a benchmarking program. What remains is the accounting. If either exchangeability condition fails, source outcomes and target covariates alone cannot generally identify the resulting bias or apportion it between the two conditions, and no reporting practice attempts either.
problems.why_open: Both assumption sets are untestable and they fail in correlated ways: a health system whose case mix differs is usually also one whose confounding structure and treatment availability differ, so a single sensitivity parameter cannot represent the joint failure and separate parameters are not separately identified. Unmeasured effect modification is undetectable in the source population by construction. Combining transport with flexible representation learning risks erasing the effect modification transport is meant to preserve, because predictive invariance and causal invariance are different properties.
problems.proposed_direction: Develop causal representation learning for transportability that balances populations only on representations sufficient for effect modification rather than on everything predictive, combined with targeted standardization and site-level random effects. Derive bounds under unmeasured effect modification and report them with the point estimate, so a transported number carries its own fragility rather than inheriting the source's precision. Simulate populations that differ in covariates, treatment mechanisms, baseline hazards and effect modifiers separately, so each source of non-transportability is measurable rather than confounded with the others.

problems.original_statement: Hazard ratios, odds ratios and model coefficients are routinely presented without naming the intervention, the population, the time horizon or the strategy for each intercurrent event. ICH E9(R1) and the TARGET statement both require that objectives, estimands and sensitivity analyses be aligned, and applied reporting has not caught up. The concrete failure is specific rather than general: a reader sees a hazard ratio and infers an intention-to-treat contrast, while the analysis in fact estimated a per-protocol effect, weighted for informative censoring, among the subset of patients whose observed treatment stayed compatible with a strategy during a grace period. Those are different quantities in different populations and nothing in the presentation distinguishes them.
problems.correction_note: The population named in the original was wrong, and the error matters because it is the error the entry accuses others of. Correct clone-censor weighting does not target the subset whose treatment stayed compatible: the weights reweight uncensored clone-time observations to stand for the artificially censored ones, so the contrast is in the baseline eligible population under the specified strategies. Where censoring enforces adherence the contrast is per-protocol, and the population is still the eligible one.
problems.statement: Hazard ratios, odds ratios and model coefficients are routinely presented without naming the intervention, the population, the time horizon or the strategy for each intercurrent event. ICH E9(R1) and the TARGET statement both require that objectives, estimands and sensitivity analyses be aligned, and applied reporting has not caught up. A correctly executed clone-censor-weight analysis with a grace period estimates a marginal contrast between prespecified strategies in the baseline eligible population, and where the artificial censoring enforces adherence that contrast is per-protocol. A bare hazard ratio discloses none of this: not the intervention, not the strategies, not the population, not the horizon, not the handling of intercurrent events. It is therefore read as an intention-to-treat contrast by default, and nothing in the presentation contradicts that reading.
problems.why_open: The hazard ratio survives every methodological improvement beneath it, so better estimation does not change what gets read. Stating the estimand precisely requires naming the strategies and the horizon, and the horizon is a commitment most analyses would rather not defend. The estimand vocabulary and the absolute-risk alternatives both exist and are used in methodological work; what does not exist is a requirement that an applied emulation use them, so the practice is a reporting convention rather than a capability gap.
problems.proposed_direction: Require a one-sentence estimand statement naming the intervention, the strategies, the population, the horizon and the intercurrent-event handling, positioned before any effect measure. Report absolute risks, risk differences and restricted mean outcomes at clinically meaningful horizons, with the hazard ratio as a supplement rather than the headline. Include a timeline diagram showing treatment paths and censoring rules, since a cloning-and-censoring design is easier to draw than to describe.
